Dear Professor Brown,

I am writing on behalf of the Student Union of our university to invite you to organize a team for the International Innovation Contest, which will be held on our campus from October 15 to 20.

The contest welcomes teams of three to five university students, who will present innovative solutions to environmental problems. Experts from several countries will serve as judges, and the winning teams will receive awards and chances for further cooperation. Your participation would make the contest more international and rewarding.

If you are interested, please reply by August 31. We will cover your accommodation during the contest.

Yours sincerely,
Li Ming

answer:
As shown in the picture, two female students are standing in front of a bulletin board on which a campus lecture is announced. One of them says, "It has nothing to do with our major, so it is useless to attend." The other, however, believes that listening to it will surely do them good.

The contrast between the two girls reflects two attitudes toward learning. The first girl holds a narrow view, valuing only knowledge directly related to her major. The second girl, by contrast, is open-minded and eager to broaden her horizons. In today's world, many problems are solved by combining ideas from different fields, and employers increasingly value people with wide knowledge. A lecture outside one's major may spark new ideas, sharpen critical thinking and even reveal new interests.

Therefore, I side with the second girl. As college students, we should not limit ourselves to the textbooks of our own major. Instead, we should make good use of lectures and other resources on campus to enrich ourselves. After all, the more widely we learn, the better prepared we will be for the future.
